title: Kinds of plants: trees, shrubs, herbs, climbers, creepers, and how we use them

summary.text: This unit is about the many kinds of plants around us. We sort plants mostly by their stem. A tree has one thick, hard, woody trunk. A shrub has several woody stems from near the ground. A herb has a soft green stem. A climber holds on to something to grow up, and a creeper spreads along the ground. People use plants for almost everything: food, medicine, shade, wood, cloth, rope and paper. But the boxes are ours, not the plants'. A banana plant has no wood at all, bamboo is a giant grass, and scientists still find new kinds of plants every year.
summary.art: A street corner in an Indian town: a big neem tree, a hibiscus bush, a pot of mint, a money plant climbing a pole and a pumpkin vine spreading over a wall, each with a small label.

intro.hook: Look out of the window or step outside. Count every plant you can see in one minute. Now look again. Are they all the same kind of plant? Which one could you climb? Which one could you squash between two fingers?
intro.text: About 350 years ago, a Dutch governor in Kerala wanted a giant book of every plant in Malabar. His painters drew a jackfruit tree with strings of pepper hanging from it. But a jackfruit tree does not make pepper. So where did the pepper come from? In this unit you find out. You learn to tell a tree from a shrub, a herb, a climber and a creeper, just by looking at its stem. And you find out how many things in your home came from a plant.
intro.art: A young painter in an old-fashioned coat sketching a jackfruit tree, with a thin green vine of pepper berries climbing up its trunk.

outcomes: I can sort plants into trees, shrubs, herbs, climbers and creepers, and say which part of the stem told me.
I can test stems fairly to tell soft stems from woody ones, and record what I find in a table.
I can explain why some plants climb or creep instead of standing up on their own.
I can name many ways people use plants: food, medicine, shade, wood, cloth, rope, paper and more.
I can measure and compare, for example how much cooler it is in a tree's shade, and show it in a bar chart.
I can say what scientists agree about kinds of plants, and give plants that do not fit the boxes.
I can go deep: wood took millions of years to appear, trees grew from many different plant families, and nobody knows how many plants are still undiscovered.

terms.meaning: A living thing that usually stays in one place, has green leaves and makes its own food using sunlight.
terms.example: Grass, a neem tree and the tulsi in a pot are all plants.
terms.art: A row of plants from tiny to huge: a grass blade, a tulsi pot, a hibiscus bush and a neem tree.

terms.meaning: The part of a plant that holds it up. It carries water and food between the roots and the leaves.
terms.example: A coriander stalk is a soft stem. A tree trunk is a big hard stem.
terms.art: A coriander stalk next to a slice of tree trunk, both labelled stem.

terms.meaning: Hard and stiff like wood. A woody stem does not bend or squash easily.
terms.example: A neem twig is woody. It snaps when you bend it too far.
terms.art: A hand bending a twig that snaps with a crack.

terms.meaning: A big plant with one thick, hard, woody stem called a trunk. Its branches start high up.
terms.example: Neem, mango, peepal and banyan are trees.
terms.art: A neem tree with its single trunk and branches high above a child.

terms.meaning: The one thick woody stem of a tree.
terms.example: You can hug the trunk of a mango tree.
terms.art: A child hugging a wide tree trunk, arms not meeting.

terms.meaning: The hard outer covering of a trunk or branch. It protects the tree, like our skin protects us.
terms.example: Rub your hand on a tree trunk. The rough part you feel is bark.
terms.art: A close-up of cracked brown bark with a hand resting on it.

terms.meaning: A medium-sized bushy plant. It has several hard, woody stems growing from close to the ground.
terms.example: Hibiscus, rose, mehendi and old tulsi plants are shrubs.
terms.art: A hibiscus bush with several woody stems rising from the soil.

terms.meaning: A small plant with a soft, green stem that does not become woody.
terms.example: Mint, coriander, spinach and tomato plants are herbs.
terms.art: A pot of mint and a coriander plant with soft green stems.

terms.meaning: A kind of herb with long, thin, flat leaves. Rice, wheat, sugarcane and bamboo are grasses.
terms.example: The doob grass on a lawn and the wheat in a field are grasses.
terms.art: Doob grass, a wheat stalk and a tall bamboo, side by side.

terms.meaning: A plant with a thin, bendy stem that grows upward by holding on to something, like a wall, a stick or another plant.
terms.example: Money plant, jasmine, pepper and bitter gourd are climbers.
terms.art: A money plant climbing a wooden pole with little roots.

terms.meaning: A plant with a thin, bendy stem that spreads along the ground.
terms.example: Pumpkin, watermelon and sweet potato plants are creepers.
terms.art: A pumpkin vine with big leaves spreading across the ground.

terms.meaning: A thin, curly thread that some climbers wrap around things to hold on.
terms.example: A bitter gourd plant holds the fence with its tendrils.
terms.art: A curly green tendril wrapped twice around a string.

terms.meaning: The hard material inside trunks and branches. It is made from the walls of millions of tiny dead cells, packed together.
terms.example: Your table, a pencil and a cricket bat are made of wood.
terms.art: A cut log showing rings, next to a pencil and a cricket bat.

terms.meaning: Something that helps the body get better or stay well. Many medicines first came from plants.
terms.example: Aspirin, a common pain medicine, was first made from a chemical found in willow bark.
terms.art: A willow branch next to a medicine bottle, joined by an arrow.

terms.meaning: A long, thin thread, often from a plant, that can be spun into cloth or twisted into rope.
terms.example: Cotton fibre makes your T-shirt. Coconut fibre, called coir, makes doormats and ropes.
terms.art: A cotton boll, a coconut husk with coir and a jute sack.

terms.meaning: A cooler, darker place where something blocks the sunlight.
terms.example: On a hot day, cows and people rest in the shade of a big tree.
terms.art: Cows and a cyclist resting in the dark shade under a banyan.

terms.meaning: One kind of living thing. All neem trees belong to one species. All mango trees belong to another.
terms.example: Scientists know about 390,000 species of plants, and they still find new ones every year.
terms.art: A row of different leaves, each with a small name tag.

terms.meaning: A plant growing where people do not want it. The word is about our wishes, not about the plant.
terms.example: Grass in a vegetable patch is called a weed. The same grass on a cricket field is wanted.
terms.art: The same grass plant shown twice: in a vegetable patch labelled weed, and on a lawn labelled lawn.

explanations.definition: Botanists, the scientists who study plants, often sort plants by how they grow. The biggest clues are the stem: is it hard or soft, thick or thin, standing up or held up by something else?
explanations.description: There are hundreds of thousands of kinds of plants. To make sense of them, people sort them into groups. In Class 3 we sort them by how they grow. First, feel the stem. Is it woody, like a stick, or soft and green, like a coriander stalk? Then look at its shape. Is there one trunk, or many stems from the ground? Last, ask: can it stand up by itself, or does it climb or spread on the ground? These three questions give us five kinds: trees, shrubs, herbs, climbers and creepers.
examples: A neem has one thick, woody trunk. So it is a tree.
A hibiscus has many woody stems near the ground. So it is a shrub.
A pumpkin has a long, soft stem lying on the ground. So it is a creeper.
explanations.art: A simple sorting chart drawn as three questions with arrows: hard or soft stem? one trunk or many? stands, climbs or spreads? leading to five small plant pictures.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the unit: we sort plants into kinds mostly by looking at their stems.

explanations.definition: A tree is a big plant with one thick, hard, woody stem, called a trunk. Its branches usually start well above the ground.
explanations.description: Trees are the biggest plants. Their trunk is made of wood, which is very strong. A strong trunk lets a tree lift its leaves high above other plants, into the sunlight. Trees live a long time. Many live for a hundred years or more. The outside of the trunk is covered in bark, which protects it from insects, heat and knocks. Coconut and areca palms also have one tall trunk, so we call them trees too. But their trunk does not grow fatter every year like a mango trunk does.
examples: Neem, mango, peepal, banyan, jamun and tamarind are trees.
The coconut palm has one tall trunk and no branches. Its leaves grow from the very top.
There are about 3 trillion trees on Earth. That is about 400 trees for every person.
explanations.art: A mango tree with a child standing under it, arrows showing the trunk, the bark and the high branches.
explanations.context: This card is about trees, the biggest kind of plant.

explanations.definition: A shrub is a medium-sized, bushy plant. It has several woody stems that grow from close to the ground.
explanations.description: A shrub is smaller than a tree, usually not much taller than a grown-up. Its stems are hard and woody, like a tree's. But instead of one trunk, a shrub has many stems coming up from near the soil. This makes it look bushy. People often plant shrubs as hedges, because they grow thick and close together. Many flowering plants in Indian gardens are shrubs.
examples: Hibiscus, rose, bougainvillea, mehendi, kaner and lemon plants are shrubs.
Tulsi starts as a soft herb. As it gets older, its stem turns woody, and it becomes a small shrub.
A hedge around a park is a row of shrubs, cut into a wall shape.
explanations.art: A rose bush and a hibiscus bush, with their many woody stems coming up from the soil highlighted.
explanations.context: This card is about shrubs, the bushy plants with many woody stems.

explanations.definition: A herb is a small plant with a soft, green stem that does not turn into wood. Grasses are a special group of herbs with long, thin leaves.
explanations.description: Squeeze the stem of a coriander plant. It is soft and juicy, and it bends easily. That is a herb. Most herbs are small and many live only one season. They grow quickly, make their seeds, and die. Then the seeds grow into new plants. Grasses are herbs too. Their leaves are long and narrow, and their stems are often hollow. The food grains we eat most, like rice, wheat, maize, bajra and ragi, all come from grasses. In cooking, 'herbs' means leaves that add taste, like mint. In science, a herb is any plant with a soft stem.
examples: Mint, coriander, spinach, methi, tomato and mustard plants are herbs.
Rice, wheat, ragi, sugarcane and doob are grasses.
Bamboo is a grass too. Some bamboos grow taller than a house, but they are still grasses.
explanations.art: A mint plant, a tomato plant and a rice plant in a row, each with a soft green stem bending under a finger.
explanations.context: This card is about herbs, the plants with soft green stems, and grasses, which are a special group of herbs.

explanations.definition: A climber is a plant with a thin, weak stem that grows upward by holding on to something else, like a wall, a fence, a stick or another plant.
explanations.description: A climber's stem is too thin to stand up by itself. So it holds on to a support and climbs towards the light. Climbers hold on in different ways. Some twist their whole stem around a stick, like the bean plant. Some grow curly threads called tendrils, which wrap around things, like bitter gourd and grapes. Some grow tiny roots along the stem that press into bark or walls, like money plant and pepper. Some hook on with thorns, like bougainvillea. Climbing is clever. The plant does not spend food building a thick trunk. It uses someone else's.
examples: Money plant and pepper climb with little roots on the stem.
Bitter gourd, bottle gourd and grapes climb with tendrils.
Bean plants and morning glory climb by twisting their stem around a support.
explanations.art: Four small panels: a bean twisting up a stick, a tendril curled on a string, money plant roots gripping a pole, and bougainvillea thorns hooked on a wall.
explanations.context: This card is about climbers: plants that hold on to something to grow upward.

explanations.definition: A creeper is a plant with a long, thin, weak stem that spreads along the ground instead of standing up.
explanations.description: A creeper cannot stand up, and it has nothing to climb. So it spreads out flat over the ground. This way it covers a big area with its leaves, where they can catch the sunlight. Many creepers grow new roots wherever their stem touches the soil. So one creeper can slowly cover a whole patch. Big fruits like pumpkins and watermelons are too heavy to hang from a thin stem in the air. Lying on the ground, the stem does not have to hold them up. Some plants can do both. A pumpkin creeps on the ground, but if it finds a wall it will climb it.
examples: Pumpkin, watermelon, cucumber and sweet potato plants are creepers.
Doob grass creeps along the ground and grows roots as it goes.
A strawberry plant sends out long stems along the ground, and new baby plants grow at their tips.
explanations.art: A watermelon creeper spreading across sandy ground, with a big striped watermelon resting on the soil and small roots where the stem touches the ground.
explanations.context: This card is about creepers: plants that spread along the ground.

explanations.concept: Why climb? Why creep? The race for light
explanations.definition: Plants need sunlight to make their food. Trees, shrubs, herbs, climbers and creepers are different ways of reaching that light.
explanations.description: Think of a crowded forest. Every plant needs sunlight. The tallest plants get it first, and the ones below are in shade. A tree wins the race by building a tall trunk. But wood is costly. The tree spends a lot of its food, year after year, to build it. A herb does the opposite. It grows fast, makes seeds and is done in a few months. A climber uses a trick. It grows a thin, cheap stem and leans on a tree, so it reaches the top without building a trunk. A creeper spreads sideways and catches light in open spaces. No way is the best. Each one works in its own place.
examples: In a forest, giant climbers called lianas can reach the very top of the trees.
On a sunny open field, creepers like doob grass cover the ground.
In a dark, crowded garden corner, a money plant climbs towards the window.
explanations.art: A forest drawn as a race: a tall tree, a vine climbing it, a shrub halfway up, and a creeper on a sunny clearing, all reaching for a sun.
explanations.context: This card explains why plants grow in such different ways: they are all reaching for sunlight.

explanations.description: Our five kinds are useful, but nature does not always fit them. A banana plant looks like a tree. But it has no wood at all. Its 'trunk' is made of leaf bottoms rolled tightly around each other, so botanists call it a giant herb. Bamboo grows as tall as a tree, but it is a grass. Tulsi starts soft, like a herb, and becomes woody, like a shrub. Papaya has a single trunk, but its wood is soft and spongy. Some plants, like the pumpkin, creep or climb, depending on what they find. So scientists use the five kinds as a handy guide, not as walls.
examples: A banana plant can be taller than a grown-up, but you can cut through its stem with a kitchen knife, because there is no wood.
Some bamboos can grow almost a metre in one day.
The same lantana plant can grow as a shrub in an open field, or climb up into trees at the forest edge.

perspectives.who: Many botanists who sort plants by how they grow
perspectives.explanation: Life forms, like tree and climber, are real and useful. They tell you how a plant lives and wins light. In 1904 a Danish botanist, Christen Raunkiaer, made a famous system of plant life forms that is still used.

perspectives.who: Botanists who sort plants by family
perspectives.explanation: How a plant grows tells you little about who it is related to. A rose and an apple tree are close cousins, but one is a shrub and one is a tree. So for finding relatives, scientists compare flowers, seeds and genes, not stems.

explanations.art: A banana plant cut open, showing rolled leaf layers inside its stem, next to a bamboo taller than a house, both with question marks.
explanations.context: This card is about plants that do not fit neatly into tree, shrub, herb, climber or creeper.

explanations.definition: Wood is the hard part of trunks and branches. It is made from the stiff walls of millions of tiny, long cells that have died and stayed in place.
explanations.description: A plant's body is made of tiny living units called cells. In a woody stem, many cells build thick, tough walls around themselves. Two materials make the walls strong. One is cellulose, the same stuff as in cotton and paper. The other is lignin, which works like a hard glue. When these cells die, their walls stay, packed together like a bundle of straws. That is wood. Each year, many trees add a new layer of wood just under the bark. In places with a cold winter or a long dry season, these layers show as rings. Many trees in the warm tropics have rings that are hard to read.
examples: A soft herb stem has very little lignin, so it bends and squashes.
Teak, sheesham and sal wood are hard and strong, so people make furniture and doors from them.
Paper is made from wood with most of the lignin taken out, leaving the soft cellulose.
explanations.art: A zoom in three steps: a log, the rings, then a bundle of tiny tube-shaped cells with thick walls.
explanations.context: This card zooms into a tree trunk to find out what wood really is.

explanations.concept: Wood took millions of years to appear
explanations.definition: The first plants on land had no wood. Woody stems and the first trees appeared about 400 to 385 million years ago.
explanations.description: For most of Earth's history there were no plants on land at all. The first land plants were tiny, like moss, and lay close to the ground. Over millions of years, some plants found how to make lignin, the hard glue in wood. Now they could stand tall. The oldest known fossil forest was found at Gilboa, in New York State. Its trees lived about 385 million years ago, long before dinosaurs. They looked like giant ferns on top of a trunk. Wood changed the whole planet. Forests spread, made soil and changed the air.
examples: The Gilboa fossil forest trees, called Wattieza, were about 8 metres tall.
Coal is the squashed remains of ancient forests and swamps from about 300 million years ago.
Before trees, the tallest things on land were strange living pillars called Prototaxites. They may have been giant fungi.
explanations.art: An ancient landscape with fern-topped early trees, and a small modern child standing in a corner for size.
explanations.context: This card goes back in time, to when the first trees grew on Earth.

explanations.definition: Being a tree is a way of growing, not a family. Plants from many unrelated families have become trees on their own.
explanations.description: You might think all trees are close cousins. They are not. Many very different plant families found the trick of growing a tall trunk, separately, at different times. A pine, a coconut palm and a mango are all trees, but they are distant relatives. The coconut is closer to rice and bamboo than to the mango. Scientists have also found the opposite. Some families of herbs came from woody ancestors, and on some islands, herbs turned back into woody shrubs and trees. So 'tree' describes what a plant does, not which family it belongs to.
examples: Coconut palms are related to grasses, not to mango trees.
There are about 73,000 kinds of trees, from hundreds of different plant families.
On the Canary Islands, some plants whose relatives are soft herbs grow as woody shrubs.
explanations.art: A big family tree of plants where the 'tree' shape pops up in many separate branches, each marked with a little tree icon.
explanations.context: This card is about a surprising fact: trees are not one family. Many kinds of plants became trees separately.

explanations.concept: One plant or a whole forest?
explanations.description: A banyan tree drops roots from its branches. These prop roots grow thick and become new trunks. The Great Banyan in the Botanic Garden at Howrah, near Kolkata, is about 250 years old. It has thousands of prop roots and covers more ground than two football fields. Its first trunk died and was removed in 1925, but the tree lives on. So is it one tree or many? In Utah, in America, there is a grove of about 47,000 aspen trunks, called Pando. They all grow from one root system, with the same genes. Some scientists call it one plant, maybe the heaviest living thing on Earth.
examples: A banyan can look like a small forest, but it is one plant.
A bamboo clump is many stems joined underground.
Doob grass on a lawn may be one plant, spread out and joined by its creeping stems.

perspectives.who: Scientists who count by genes and roots
perspectives.explanation: If every trunk has the same genes and they share one root system, it is one living thing. So Pando is one plant.
Each trunk can live on its own if the roots are cut. So each one is its own plant. The word 'individual' does not fit plants as neatly as it fits animals.

explanations.art: The Great Banyan seen from above, with hundreds of prop roots like pillars, and a tiny person walking between them.
explanations.context: This card asks a puzzling question: when many trunks share one root, is it one plant or many?

explanations.definition: People depend on plants for food, medicine, shade, wood, cloth, rope, paper, oil, colours and much more.
explanations.description: Look at your breakfast. Rice, wheat, dal, vegetables, fruit, sugar, tea and spices all come from plants. Milk comes from cows that eat grass. Almost all our food comes from plants in the end. Just three grasses, rice, wheat and maize, give the world about half of all its food energy. Your cotton clothes are made from the fluffy fibres of the cotton plant. Your chair, door and pencil are wood. The rubber in your chappal came from the milky sap of a rubber tree. Haldi and mehendi give us colours. Coconut and mustard give us oil. Trees give us shade and cool our streets.
examples: Food: rice, wheat, dal, mango, banana, tea and sugar.
Things: cotton cloth, jute bags, coir doormats, wooden furniture, paper and rubber.
Colours: haldi gives yellow, mehendi gives orange-red and indigo gives blue.
explanations.art: A plate, a T-shirt, a chair, a rubber chappal and a notebook, each with a dotted line leading back to the plant it came from.
explanations.context: This card is about all the ways people use plants, every single day.

explanations.definition: Many medicines were first found in plants. Plants make strong chemicals to protect themselves, and some of these chemicals can help us heal.
explanations.description: Plants cannot run from insects that eat them. So many plants make bitter or smelly chemicals to protect themselves. Some of these chemicals help people too. For thousands of years, people found out which plants helped with which illness. India's Charaka Samhita, an old book of Ayurveda, describes hundreds of plant medicines. Scientists today test these plants and find out what is inside them. A chemical from willow bark led to aspirin. Sadabahar, the pink periwinkle in many Indian gardens, gave two medicines for blood cancers in children. Tu Youyou, a Chinese scientist, found a malaria medicine in sweet wormwood and won a Nobel Prize in 2015. Asima Chatterjee, a chemist in Kolkata, studied Indian medicine plants for most of her life.
examples: Sadabahar (periwinkle) gave the cancer medicines vincristine and vinblastine.
Sweet wormwood gave artemisinin, a medicine that has saved millions from malaria.
Willow bark has a chemical called salicin. Chemists changed it slightly to make aspirin in 1897.
explanations.art: A garden sadabahar plant with pink flowers, linked by an arrow to a small medicine bottle, and a scientist with a notebook beside it.
explanations.context: This card is about medicines that people first found in plants. Never eat or taste a plant to test it.

explanations.definition: Some plants make chemicals strong enough to make people very ill. A plant being natural does not make it safe.
explanations.description: The same chemicals that protect a plant from insects can hurt us. Kaner, also called oleander, is a common shrub along Indian roads and gardens. Every part of it is very poisonous. Castor seeds and datura are poisonous too. Even plants that help as medicines can harm if a person takes the wrong part or too much. That is why we never eat or taste a wild plant, leaf, seed or berry without a grown-up who truly knows it. Scientists and doctors test plant medicines carefully, to find the right amount.
examples: Kaner (oleander) is poisonous in every part, even though it is planted everywhere for its flowers.
Castor seeds are poisonous to eat, even though castor oil is made from them by a careful process.
Wash your hands after handling plants you do not know.
explanations.art: A kaner shrub with pink flowers and a clear 'do not eat' sign drawn as a crossed-out mouth, no words.
explanations.context: This card is a safety card. It is about plants that are poisonous.

explanations.concept: Shade: how trees cool a street
explanations.definition: Trees cool the air and ground around them in two ways. Their leaves block sunlight, and they give off water from their leaves, which cools the air.
explanations.description: Stand on a road in the afternoon sun. Then step under a big tree. You feel the difference at once. First, the leaves catch the sunlight before it reaches the ground, so the ground stays cooler. Second, leaves give off water as an invisible vapour. Turning water into vapour takes heat away, the same way sweat cools your skin. A big tree gives off a lot of water on a hot day. Streets with many trees can be several degrees cooler than streets with none. In summer, the ground in the sun can be far hotter than the ground in shade.
examples: Cows, dogs and auto drivers all choose the shade of a tree on a hot afternoon.
Old roads in India were planted with lines of trees, like banyan, neem and mango, to shade travellers.
A sunny tiled roof can get too hot to touch, while a creeper-covered wall stays cool.
explanations.art: A hot road with a thermometer in the sun showing a high red level, and a second thermometer in a tree's shade showing a lower level.
explanations.context: This card explains why it feels cooler under a tree.

explanations.concept: People who stood up for trees
explanations.definition: Many people, often women from villages, have protected trees and forests because their lives and their families depended on them.
explanations.description: In 1730, at Khejarli in Rajasthan, the king's men came to cut khejri trees. Amrita Devi, a woman of the Bishnoi community, hugged a tree to stop them. She and more than 360 Bishnoi people were killed, the story says, and the king then banned tree cutting in their villages. In 1974, in the village of Reni in the Himalayas, Gaura Devi led the women to hug trees to stop loggers. This was part of the Chipko movement. In Karnataka, Saalumarada Thimmakka and her husband planted and cared for hundreds of banyan trees along a road. In Kenya, Wangari Maathai started a movement that planted tens of millions of trees, and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2004.
examples: Chipko means 'to cling' or 'to hug' in Hindi.
Saalumarada means 'row of trees' in Kannada. Thimmakka received the Padma Shri in 2019.
Khejri trees give shade, fodder for animals and food in the desert.
explanations.art: Village women in the Himalayas hugging tree trunks in a circle, with mountains behind them.
explanations.context: This card is about people who protected trees, and why they did it.

explanations.concept: How many kinds of plants are there?
explanations.description: Scientists know about 390,000 species of plants. About 2,000 new ones are named every year. India alone has many thousands of kinds of flowering plants. We do not know the true total, because many plants grow in places few botanists have visited, like the tops of rainforest trees or remote hills. Scientists think that about 2 in every 5 plant species may be in danger of dying out, as forests are cut and the climate changes. Some may disappear before anyone has even named them.
examples: New plant species are still found in India, in places like the Western Ghats and the north-east.
There may be 9,000 kinds of trees that nobody has named yet.
Seed banks, like the one at Kew in England and the one in Svalbard in Norway, store seeds to keep plants safe.
explanations.art: A botanist with a hand lens in a misty forest, looking at a small unknown flower, with a notebook marked with a big question mark.
explanations.context: This card is about something nobody knows yet: how many kinds of plants there really are.

agreed.text: Plants can be sorted by how they grow: trees, shrubs, herbs, climbers and creepers. Grasses are a special group of herbs.
agreed.evidence: Botanists everywhere use these groups, and anyone can check them by looking at a plant's stem.

agreed.text: Woody stems are hard because their cells have thick walls with lignin in them.
agreed.evidence: Under a microscope, wood is seen as packed, thick-walled dead cells. Chemists can measure the lignin.

agreed.text: Almost all the food people and animals eat comes from plants in the end.
agreed.evidence: Follow any food chain back far enough. It always starts with a plant, or with tiny plant-like living things in the sea.

agreed.text: Many medicines were first found in plants.
agreed.evidence: Aspirin, artemisinin, vincristine and many more were found by studying plants, and then tested on patients.

agreed.text: Trees make the ground and air cooler around them.
agreed.evidence: Thermometers in the shade of trees read lower than those in the sun, and cities with more trees measure cooler.

agreed.text: Trees appeared on Earth about 385 million years ago, and plants from many different families became trees separately.
agreed.evidence: Fossil forests, like the one at Gilboa, and the family trees scientists build by comparing plant genes.

challenging.claim: A banana plant is a tree.
challenging.who: Most people, and many children's books.
challenging.for: It is tall, and it has one thick trunk with big leaves at the top.
challenging.against: Its trunk has no wood at all. It is made of rolled-up leaf bottoms. When it fruits, the whole stem dies. So botanists call it a giant herb.
challenging.context: This card is about a plant everyone thinks is a tree: the banana.

challenging.claim: Plants exist for people to use.
challenging.who: Aristotle, a Greek thinker who lived about 2,350 years ago, wrote that plants exist for the sake of animals, and animals for the sake of people. Many people still feel this way.
challenging.for: People really do use plants for almost everything, and farming has fed billions of people.
challenging.against: Plants lived on Earth for hundreds of millions of years before any people. Most plants are never used by people at all. Scientists say plants live for themselves, and many living things depend on them.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea: that plants are here for us.

challenging.claim: A weed is a bad kind of plant.
challenging.for: Some plants spread fast and take water and light from crops. A few, like congress grass, can harm people and animals.
challenging.against: 'Weed' just means a plant growing where we do not want it. The same grass is a weed in a vegetable patch and a lawn on a cricket field. Many 'weeds' feed bees and butterflies or hold soil in place.
challenging.context: This card asks whether there is really such a thing as a weed.

challenging.claim: Natural plant medicines are always safe.
challenging.for: People have used some plant remedies for a very long time.
challenging.against: Some plants, like kaner and datura, are deadly. Even helpful plants can harm in the wrong amount. That is why plant medicines must be tested carefully, like any medicine.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that anything natural must be safe.

challenging.who: A very natural idea, because trees look alike.
challenging.for: Most trees share the same body plan: one trunk, branches and leaves.
challenging.against: When scientists compare genes, they find that trees come from many separate plant families. A coconut palm is closer to rice than to a mango tree.
challenging.context: This card is about whether all trees belong to one family.

challenging.claim: Trees in a forest share food and messages through fungi under the ground, like a 'wood wide web'.
challenging.who: Suzanne Simard, a Canadian forest scientist, and many popular books.
challenging.for: In 1997, Simard and her team showed that some carbon passed between trees through fungi joined to their roots.
challenging.against: In 2023, other scientists looked again at the studies. They said the evidence that trees really help each other this way is weaker than the popular story says.
challenging.context: This card is about a big argument in forest science today.

big_questions.q: Is a banana plant a tree? Who decides what counts as a tree?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a tree's trunk is made of. Then think about who made up the word 'tree'.

big_questions.q: Why doesn't every plant grow into a big tree, if trees get the most light?
big_questions.hint: Wood costs a plant a lot of food. What could a plant do with that food instead?

big_questions.q: A climber leans on a tree to reach the light. Is that fair to the tree? Is it sharing or stealing?
big_questions.hint: Does the tree lose anything? What if the climber grows very heavy?

big_questions.q: When many trunks grow from one root, like a banyan, is it one plant or many?
big_questions.hint: What makes you one person? Is it your body, your genes, or something else?

big_questions.q: Could people live on Earth without plants? Could plants live without people?
big_questions.hint: Think about food, air, clothes and shade. Then think about what plants needed before people existed.

big_questions.q: Who decides whether a plant is a weed?
big_questions.hint: Is it the plant, the bee that visits it, or the person who owns the garden?

big_questions.q: Healers in villages knew about medicine plants long before scientists tested them. Who should get the credit, and who should get paid, when a medicine is made?
big_questions.hint: Think of the healer, the scientist who tested it and the company that sells it.

big_questions.q: If you could ask a plant, would it want to be useful to us?
big_questions.hint: Some plants, like mango, grew tastier because people chose the best ones for thousands of years.

big_questions.q: Why do so many cultures think certain trees are special, like the peepal, the banyan or the khejri?
big_questions.hint: Think of how old these trees can be, how big, and what they give to people and animals.

big_questions.q: How many kinds of plants exist that nobody has ever seen?
big_questions.hint: Where on Earth do few people go? What might grow there?

big_questions.q: Wood stores the energy of sunlight for years. When we burn wood, where does that energy go?
big_questions.hint: Hold your hands near a fire. What do you feel? Where did that warmth start?

story.title: The Pepper Tree That Wasn't
story.note: The book is real. Hortus Malabaricus, 'The Garden of Malabar', was made for the Dutch governor Hendrik van Rheede and printed in Amsterdam in 12 volumes between 1678 and 1693. Itty Achuden, a healer from the Ezhava community, really was its main plant expert, and his statement in Malayalam really is printed in the first volume. Ranga Bhat, Vinayaka Pandit and Appu Bhat really helped too. Kunjan, Pieter and the pepper drawing are made up.
text: In the year 1675, when I was nine years old, a Dutch governor in Kochi decided he wanted to know every plant in Malabar. His name was Hendrik van Rheede. He wanted a book so big and so true that nobody in Europe would ever again have to guess what grew on our coast. But a governor cannot learn a thousand plants by himself. So he sent for my uncle.

My uncle was Itty Achuden. He was a vaidyan, a healer, from a village by the sea, south of Kochi. He knew plants the way other people know their cousins. He knew them by their leaves and their bark, by their smell when you crushed them, and by the way they grew. He carried palm-leaf books that his family had copied and recopied for longer than anyone could remember. Three learned men came too: Ranga Bhat, Vinayaka Pandit and Appu Bhat, who knew the old Sanskrit books of healing. But when the governor wanted to see a plant alive, it was my uncle who walked out and found it.

My job was small. I carried the baskets. I held leaves flat on the table while the painters drew them. The painters were young Dutchmen with ink on their cuffs and sweat on their noses. The youngest was called Pieter. Pieter was the one who could not find the pepper.

This seemed very funny to me, and also a little sad. The Dutch had sailed halfway round the world for pepper. Their ships left Kochi so full of black pepper that the sailors said they could smell it from the mast. Pieter had eaten pepper every day of his life. But he had never once seen it growing.
'The governor wants the pepper tree drawn first,' he told me, through the man who changed his words into ours. 'The whole tree. Roots, flowers, fruit, everything.'

For three days Pieter walked the gardens with his paper and his pens. He looked at every tree. He drew the coconut palms, tall and bare, with their leaves bursting out at the very top. He drew the mango, round and dark like a crowd of people standing close. He drew the tamarind, the drumstick and the neem. He drew the jackfruit, with its huge spiky fruits growing straight out of the trunk, as if the tree had forgotten to grow branches for them. Not one of them had a single peppercorn.

On the fourth day he came back cross. He spread a drawing on the floor of our verandah. It was a jackfruit tree, beautifully done. And hanging among its thick, shiny leaves were long, thin strings of little green berries, like beads on a thread.
'There,' he said. 'Pepper growing on a jackfruit tree. Your uncle says it is wrong. He says a jackfruit cannot make pepper. Then where do the berries come from?'

Uncle only smiled, and said, 'Kunjan will show you.' He liked to let people find things for themselves. He said a thing you find stays with you, and a thing you are told falls out of your pocket on the way home.

So I took Pieter back to the garden behind the market, where he had sat drawing. I walked up to the jackfruit tree and put my hand flat on its trunk. The bark was rough and warm. 'This is one plant,' I said. Then I moved my hand a little to one side, onto a thin green rope pressed tight against the bark. 'And this is another.'

The rope was a stem. It was no thicker than my finger. It wandered up the trunk in a long, crooked line. Every little way along it, there were tiny brown roots. They were pushed into the cracks of the bark, like fingers holding on to a wall. Its leaves were not jackfruit leaves at all. They were shaped like hearts, glossy and pointed, with lines running from the stalk to the tip. And up in the branches, the strings of berries hung from that thin stem, not from the tree.
Pieter stared. He touched the stem. He tugged it, gently, and it held on.
'It has no trunk,' he said slowly.
'It doesn't need one,' I said. 'The jackfruit made the trunk. The pepper climbs it.'

Then I told him what every child in our village knew. When people plant pepper, they never plant it alone. First they plant a tree, or set a strong post in the ground. Then they plant the pepper at its foot. The pepper stem is soft and bendy. Left on the ground, it creeps about in the shade and gives you hardly a handful of berries. Give it something to hold, and up it goes, towards the sun, gripping with its little roots all the way.

'Then I have drawn two plants as if they were one,' said Pieter. He looked at his picture for a long time. I thought he would be ashamed. Instead, he laughed, so loudly that a crow flew off the wall. 'All the way from Amsterdam,' he said, 'to find out that pepper is a climber.'

That evening he made a new drawing. This time he drew only the pepper. He drew the thin stem, the clinging roots, the heart-shaped leaves and the hanging strings of berries. He left the jackfruit out completely. On the page, the stem went straight up the paper with nothing to hold it, like a rope climbing into the sky.
Uncle looked at the drawing for a long time. 'It is correct,' he said at last. 'But it is also strange. Nobody has ever seen pepper growing alone like that.'
Pieter thought about this. Then he dipped his pen and, very lightly, at the edge of the page, drew a single strip of rough bark. 'There,' he said. 'Now it remembers what it leans on.'

Many years later, the governor's book was printed far away in Amsterdam. It came in twelve great volumes, with hundreds of drawings of the plants of our coast. In the very first volume, there is a page printed in our own Malayalam letters. It is my uncle's statement, telling every reader who he was, and how he knew these plants. Most people who open that book look only at the pictures. I always look for that page first.

And now, when I see a coconut palm with a green vine winding up it, or a jackfruit wrapped in heart-shaped leaves, I do not see one plant. I see two lives making one shape. One stands. One climbs. Both of them are reaching for the same sun.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the pepper is not part of the jackfruit tree. It is a climber, a plant with a thin, soft stem that cannot stand up alone. So it holds on to a tree and climbs to the light, gripping with little roots. Knowing the kind of plant tells you where to look and what you are seeing. The story also quietly asks who gets remembered in a famous book: the governor, the painters, or the healer who knew the plants.
ask: Why couldn't Pieter find a 'pepper tree' anywhere?
How does the pepper plant hold on to the jackfruit tree?
What happens to a pepper plant if it has nothing to climb?
Uncle said 'Kunjan will show you' instead of explaining. Why do you think he did that?
The book was the governor's idea, but the plant knowledge was Itty Achuden's. Whose name do you think should be on the cover?
